0.title: Holy Exiles: Living the Gospel Under Pressure
0.overview:
First Peter is the New Testament's sustained theology of exile. Peter writes to Christians scattered across five provinces of Asia Minor — Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia — identifying them with three words that frame everything: elect, resident aliens, of the Dispersion. They are chosen by God and displaced in the world. These two facts stand in permanent tension throughout the letter: you are precious beyond calculation to the God who elected you; you are strangers and foreigners in the world you inhabit. Both are true at the same time, and both must shape how you live.

The recipients were primarily Gentiles — 2:10 quotes Hosea's 'not a people' passage, and 4:3 describes their former lives as pagan. Yet Peter addresses them with the vocabulary of Israel: elect exiles of the Dispersion, a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation. The church has stepped into the covenant identity of Israel and now carries it into a hostile empire. The suffering they face — social ostracism, slander, economic disadvantage, possibly intermittent persecution — is the normal cost of that identity. The letter does not explain why suffering comes; it explains how to endure it and what it means.

The letter's Christological center is 2:21–25 and 3:18–22: Christ's own suffering, death, resurrection, and ascension are the template for Christian existence. He suffered unjustly; he did not retaliate; he entrusted himself to the one who judges justly; he was vindicated. The pattern is not merely an example to follow but a participation to enter: believers share Christ's sufferings (4:13) so that they will share his glory. The theology of suffering in 1 Peter is not stoic endurance but eschatological confidence — the same confidence that carried Jesus through the cross to resurrection is available to every believer in every form of suffering.

Did Peter really write this letter, given its polished Greek? Many scholars think a later follower wrote it, pointing to the style, unlikely from a Galilean fisherman, and to a setting of persecution they date later. But the letter claims Peter as author (1:1; 5:1), the early church received it without doubt, and Peter says he wrote By Silvanus (5:12), most likely Silas, Paul’s companion, who helped with the writing. The persecution described fits the 60s under Nero, and a fisherman from bilingual Galilee who had preached for thirty years could well write good Greek with help. The more likely conclusion is that Peter wrote it from Rome, the Babylon of 5:13, before his death around AD 64–67.

The letter was written from 'Babylon' (5:13) — the Jewish-Christian code word for Rome, used also in 4 Ezra and Revelation. Silvanus (Silas) may have served as secretary (5:12), which would explain the polished Greek that would be surprising from a Galilean fisherman. The likely date is 62–64 AD, during or shortly before the Neronian persecution that would claim both Peter and Paul.

1.title: Living Hope: Election, Holiness, and the Imperishable Word
1.overview:
Chapter 1 lays the foundations of the letter. The greeting packs election, the work of the Trinity and covenant identity into two verses. The thanksgiving (vv. 3–12) shows why Christians have hope: God has given new birth to a living hope through Christ’s resurrection, and an inheritance kept in heaven, while he guards his people until it is revealed. Suffering on the way does not contradict that hope; it tests and proves it.

Then comes the call to holiness (vv. 13–25). Because of who you now are, live accordingly: “You shall be holy, for I am holy.” The standard is God himself, and the motive is the price of our ransom, the precious blood of Christ. The chapter ends with the word of God, which gave us new birth and remains when everything else withers.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter writes to “elect exiles” scattered across five Roman provinces. They are chosen by God the Father, set apart by the Spirit, for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling with his blood. Chosen and strangers, both at once.
verseByVerse.theology:
Elect Exiles

Chosen by God and strangers in the world — both at once, and the second is no evidence against the first. Father, Spirit and Son are all at work in their salvation.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Scattered believers across five provinces were being slandered and excluded.

Now: Being out of place in the world is no sign that God has forgotten you.

verseByVerse.quote: Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who are elect exiles of the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in the sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience to Jesus Christ and for sprinkling with his blood: May grace and peace be multiplied to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter writes to God’s chosen people, scattered as foreigners across much of modern Turkey, chosen by the Father’s foreknowledge, made holy by the Spirit, to obey Jesus Christ and be cleansed by his blood. He prays that grace and peace will abound to them.

Elect exiles. The highest status beside the lowest. Elect: chosen, God’s own, Israel’s language. Exiles: resident foreigners with no standing. Peter says both are true, and the second is no evidence against the first. These believers were slandered and excluded, and might have thought God had forgotten them. Peter refuses that conclusion in his first sentence.

Father, Spirit, Son. The origin is the Father’s foreknowledge, the means the Spirit’s sanctifying work, the goal obedience to Christ and cleansing by his blood. One salvation, three persons.

What “foreknowledge” means. Some read it as God foreseeing who would choose him, and choosing them in response. But in Scripture, for God to “know” someone is to set his love on them: “You only have I known of all the families of the earth” (Amos 3:2). Peter uses the same word of Christ, “foreknown before the foundation of the world” (1:20), which cannot mean God foresaw Christ’s choice. It is love fixed beforehand.

Sprinkled. This recalls Exodus 24:8, where blood was thrown on the people and Israel became God’s covenant nation. The same has happened to these Gentile exiles.

On a Tuesday. A believer moves abroad for work and feels like an outsider in every room. Peter would say: you are an exile, and you are chosen. Being out of place in the world is no sign that God has forgotten you.
verseByVerse.note: Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia were Roman provinces covering much of modern Turkey. Peter probably wrote from Rome in the early 60s AD, shortly before Nero’s persecution. The readers were mostly Gentile believers, now “exiles” in their own society.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–12 — Born Again to a Living Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter bursts into praise. God has given his people new birth to a living hope through Christ’s resurrection, an inheritance that cannot perish, kept in heaven, while they are guarded by his power. So they rejoice, even in grief, because trials test their faith as fire tests gold. They love Christ though they have not seen him. And the prophets who foretold this grace searched to understand it, learning that they served a later generation, in things angels long to look into.
verseByVerse.theology:
Kept, and Keeping

Born again to a living hope, believers have an inheritance kept in heaven and are themselves guarded by God's power until it is revealed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The prophets searched their own words about Christ’s sufferings and the glories to follow.

Now: Trials test faith as fire tests gold, and faith is worth far more.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! According to his great mercy, he has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you, who by God's power are being guarded through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Praise God, who in his great mercy has given us new birth into a living hope through Jesus’ resurrection, and into an inheritance that can never perish, spoil or fade, kept in heaven for you, who are being guarded by God’s power through faith until salvation is revealed at the end.

Praise first. Whatever they were suffering, Peter’s first word is worship.

Born again. He caused it. No one arranges their own birth. Peter chose the image on purpose (John 3:3).

A living hope. Alive because Christ is alive. A dead man’s promises die with him; these do not.

The inheritance. Three words, each denying something that happens to earthly inheritances: it cannot decay, be polluted or fade. Many readers had lost property. This inheritance is “kept in heaven for you”.

Guarded. A military word: a garrison around a city. The inheritance is kept for you, and you are kept for it.

Does “through faith” put our safety back in our hands? No. Faith is the means by which God guards us, not a condition that makes our security depend on us. The faith itself is God’s gift, kept by his power.

On a Tuesday. A family loses their savings when a business fails. It is a real loss, and grief is right. But their true inheritance has not been touched, and the one who keeps it is guarding them too. That truth can steady them as they rebuild.

verseByVerse.quote: In this you rejoice, though now for a little while, if necessary, you have been grieved by various trials, so that the tested genuineness of your faith—more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire—may be found to result in praise and glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You rejoice in this, even though for a short time you have had to suffer many kinds of trials, so that your faith, proved genuine, more precious than gold refined by fire, may bring praise, glory and honour when Jesus Christ is revealed.

Joy with an object. They rejoice “in this”, in what God has done, not in their circumstances.

Three mercies. Now: temporary. For a little while: short beside eternity. If necessary: the trials are not random; someone is deciding.

Grieved. Peter does not pretend the joy cancels the pain. Both are true at once.

Gold and faith. Gold is refined by fire and still perishes. Faith is refined the same way and does not. The process is the same; the product is worth far more.

On a Tuesday. A man caring for his disabled son finds his faith tested daily. Some days he feels nothing but tired. Peter tells him the fire is not destroying his faith but proving it, and that on the day Christ appears, it will be found to his praise.

verseByVerse.quote: Though you have not seen him, you love him. Though you do not now see him, you believe in him and rejoice with joy that is inexpressible and filled with glory, obtaining the outcome of your faith, the salvation of your souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though you have not seen Christ, you love him; though you do not see him now, you believe in him and are filled with an inexpressible and glorious joy, as you receive the goal of your faith, the salvation of your souls.

Who is writing. Peter had seen him: fished with him, watched him transfigured, denied him while Jesus looked at him (Luke 22:61). Yet he honours those who have not seen, as Jesus did: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20:29).

Inexpressible joy. Peter has no words for it. “Filled with glory” suggests the glory of the age to come already breaking in.

Now. “Obtaining” is present tense. Salvation is being received even while the grief of v. 6 continues.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning this salvation, the prophets who prophesied about the grace that was to be yours searched and inquired carefully, inquiring what person or time the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating when he predicted the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories. It was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but you, in the things that have now been announced to you through those who preached the good news to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, things into which angels long to look.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophets who foretold this grace searched carefully to understand who and when the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing to, as he predicted Christ’s sufferings and the glories after them. God showed them they were serving not themselves but you, in what has now been preached to you by the Holy Spirit, things angels long to look into.

Searching prophets. The writers of Scripture studied their own words, trying to understand them. They were not dictation machines.

The Spirit of Christ in them. Christ, by his Spirit, spoke through the prophets before he was born.

Suffering, then glory. The prophets saw both and could not tell how they fitted together. The order became clear only when it happened.

Serving you. They were told the answer was for a later generation, and they kept writing. Anyone labouring at something whose fruit they will not see is in good company.

Angels look. The verb means to stoop and peer in, as the disciples did into the empty tomb (John 20:5). The gospel these exiles hold is something angels crane to see. That is a reason to worship.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — Be Holy, for I Am Holy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: “Therefore”: everything that follows rests on vv. 3–12. Prepare your minds, stay sober, and set your hope fully on the grace coming at Christ’s appearing. Be holy, because God who called you is holy. Live in reverent fear during your exile, remembering that you were ransomed not with silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ. Love one another earnestly, because you have been born again through the living word of God, which remains for ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Fear of a Child

Be holy, because the one who called you is holy. Call on him as Father who judges impartially, and remember the price of your ransom: the precious blood of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: These believers had been ransomed from empty ways handed down from their ancestors.

Now: All flesh withers, but the word of the Lord remains, and that word is the gospel preached to you.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, preparing your minds for action, and being sober-minded, set your hope fully on the grace that will be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So prepare your minds for action, stay clear-headed, and set your hope completely on the grace you will receive when Jesus Christ is revealed.

Girding the mind. The Greek pictures tucking a long robe into a belt before running or working. Gather up a mind that would otherwise trail and trip. It may recall the Passover, eaten ready to leave Egypt.

Sober-minded. The opposite of drunk: clear, seeing things as they are. Suffering, fear and the culture around us all distort our judgment.

Hope fully. Without reserve, with no second option held back. Peter does not promise the trials will stop. He tells them where to put their hope so that it survives if they do not.

On a Tuesday. When anxious thoughts spin late at night, “gird up your mind”: name the worry, hand it to God, and deliberately turn your thoughts to the grace that is coming. Hope is something you place, on purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: As obedient children, do not be conformed to the passions of your former ignorance, but as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, since it is written, "You shall be holy, for I am holy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As obedient children, do not be shaped by the desires you had when you did not know God. Instead, be holy in everything you do, because the God who called you is holy, as Scripture says, “You shall be holy, for I am holy.”

Do not be conformed. To be pressed into a mould from outside (Romans 12:2). The pressure is constant and mostly unnoticed.

Former ignorance. A merciful description of a pagan past: not knowing. Now they know.

The standard. Not a bit better than the culture, but God himself. Holiness means set apart, belonging to another order: a life that is visibly not from around here. And in all conduct, not just the religious parts.

Can we be holy as God is? In one sense believers already are holy, set apart as his people (2:9). In another, it is lifelong growth by the Spirit, never complete in this life (1 John 1:8). God supplies what he commands.

Leviticus applied. Peter applies Israel’s command (Leviticus 11:44) directly to Gentile believers, because they are now God’s covenant people.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you call on him as Father who judges impartially according to each one's deeds, conduct yourselves with fear throughout the time of your exile,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since you call on God as Father, who judges each person impartially by what they do, live in reverent fear during your time as foreigners.

Father and Judge. Peter holds them together. God is our Father, and he judges without favouritism. For people at the bottom of every social ladder, impartiality is good news.

What “fear” means. Not terror of condemnation; he has just called God Father, and “perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). It is reverence: knowing who you are dealing with. Fear that drives you away from God is the wrong kind; fear that keeps you careful in his presence is the right kind.

Judged by deeds? Does this contradict justification by faith alone? No. We are justified by faith alone, but justifying faith shows itself in deeds, and at the judgment those deeds are the evidence (2 Corinthians 5:10).

On a Tuesday. The fear of God is freeing. A woman afraid of her boss’s anger remembers that she answers finally to God. A person who truly fears God has little fear left for anyone else.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing that you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You know that you were set free from the empty way of life handed down by your ancestors, not with things that perish like silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, the spotless lamb.

Ransomed. The word for paying a price to release a slave or prisoner, recalling God’s rescue of Israel from Egypt.

Inherited futility. These ways came down to them; they did not choose them. That is why they needed a ransom, not just advice.

The price. Not silver or gold, the most durable currencies of the day, but the blood of Christ, like a Passover lamb inspected and found flawless.

Paid to whom? Not to Satan, who has no rightful claim. The price satisfied God’s justice (Romans 3:24–26). What we are freed from is slavery to sin and its penalty.

On a Tuesday. Someone made to feel worthless at work or at home can remember this: you can tell what something is worth by what was paid for it. You were bought with the blood of God’s Son. Let that move you to worship and to holy living.

verseByVerse.quote: He was foreknown before the foundation of the world but was made manifest in the last times for the sake of you who through him are believers in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope are in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ was chosen before the creation of the world, but has been revealed in these last times for your sake. Through him you believe in God, who raised him from the dead and glorified him, so your faith and hope are in God.

Before the world. The cross was not God’s improvised response to an emergency. The Lamb was in view before Genesis 1.

For your sake. The eternal plan was revealed for a scattered group of slandered foreigners. And for you.

Faith and hope in God. The God who raised Jesus from the dead can be trusted with your future.

verseByVerse.quote: Having purified your souls by your obedience to the truth for a sincere brotherly love, love one another earnestly from a pure heart,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since you have purified yourselves by obeying the truth, so that you have sincere love for one another, love one another deeply, from a pure heart.

Purified for love. The cleansing had a goal: love for others. “Sincere” means without a mask.

Earnestly. The word means stretched to full extent, like a muscle under strain. These churches mixed races, classes, slaves and masters. Loving such people would not happen by temperament. It would take effort, grounded in grace.

On a Tuesday. There is someone in your church you find hard to love. Peter does not tell you to feel warm towards them. He tells you to stretch: to pray for them, greet them, and do them good, because Christ has made you family.

verseByVerse.quote: since you have been born again, not of perishable seed but of imperishable, through the living and abiding word of God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have been born again, not of perishable seed but of imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God.

Family. Love one another because you share the same birth. You do not choose your siblings.

Imperishable. The third time: the inheritance (v. 4), the ransom (v. 18), and now the seed. Natural birth uses seed that dies; this birth creates a family death cannot dissolve.

Born through the word. God gives new birth (v. 3; John 3:8), and he does it through the gospel: “Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth” (James 1:18). The Spirit uses the word as his instrument. That is why the church preaches.

verseByVerse.quote: for "All flesh is like grass and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass withers, and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord remains forever." And this word is the good news that was preached to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All people are like grass, and their glory like wild flowers; the grass withers and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord lasts for ever. And this word is the good news that was preached to you.

Isaiah 40. Peter quotes a passage written to exiles, which opens, “Comfort, comfort my people.”

Glory withers. Not only human life but human splendour, the impressive part, fades. These believers were outranked by neighbours with standing; Isaiah says that standing is the most temporary thing about them.

This word. The eternal word is the very message someone preached to them. Ordinary gospel preaching carries the word that outlasts all flesh.

For worship. Everything you can see is passing. The word that gave you life is not. Build on it, and praise the God who spoke it.

2.title: Living Stones and Holy Exiles: Identity, Witness, and the Suffering Christ
2.overview:
Chapter 2 moves from who Christians are (vv. 1–10) to how they live in a hostile world (vv. 11–25). You are living stones in God’s house, a chosen race, a royal priesthood; therefore live so well among unbelievers that those who slander you will glorify God. Identity produces conduct, and conduct commends the identity.

The chapter ends with Christ’s unjust suffering (vv. 18–25). Peter frames submission not as mere social conformity but as following the suffering Servant, who entrusted himself to God, and then did what no one else could: bore our sins in his body on the tree.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Living Stones, a Royal Priesthood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Put off the sins that destroy love, and crave the pure milk of God’s word. Come to Christ, the living stone rejected by people but precious to God, and be built with other believers into one spiritual house and holy priesthood. Christ is the cornerstone to those who believe and a stumbling stone to those who disobey. And believers are now given Israel’s titles: a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s own people, called to declare his excellencies.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priesthood of All Believers

Coming to Christ, the living stone, believers are built into one spiritual house and a holy priesthood, offering sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Israel’s titles were given to Gentile converts with no status at all.

Now: Once not a people, now God’s people; once without mercy, now shown mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: So put away all malice and all deceit and hypocrisy and envy and all slander. Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk, that by it you may grow up into salvation— if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So get rid of all malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy and slander. Like newborn babies, crave the pure spiritual milk, so that you may grow up in your salvation, now that you have tasted that the Lord is good.

Put off. The verb is for taking off clothes. These belong to the old family. All five are sins against other people, and most are done with words or a false face. They make the love of 1:22 impossible.

Not among yourselves. These readers were being slandered by outsiders (2:12). Peter will not let them do to each other what is being done to them.

Crave the milk. Newborns are hungry, and loud about it. The milk is the word that gave them birth (1:23), pure, with nothing mixed in. Unlike in 1 Corinthians 3, milk here is not a beginner’s stage to outgrow, but the food that produces growth all life long.

Tasted. From Psalm 34:8. Appetite follows taste.

On a Tuesday. If you have no appetite for God’s word, do not wait to feel hungry. Read a psalm slowly, and remember a time when you tasted the Lord’s goodness. Appetite grows with eating.

verseByVerse.quote: As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious, you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As you come to Christ, the living stone rejected by people but chosen and precious to God, you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

Rejected and precious. Two verdicts on Christ, in opposite directions. The readers, rejected in their towns, are told which verdict counts.

Being built. Passive: someone is building them. And it is one house. A stone alone is rubble; it becomes a wall only set against other stones.

A priesthood. The temple had a building, priests and sacrifices, all out of ordinary people’s reach. Peter says the church is the building and the priesthood, and offers the sacrifices. This is the root of the Reformation teaching of the priesthood of all believers.

What it does not mean. It does not abolish church leadership. Every believer has direct access to God through Christ, so no priestly class is needed to offer sacrifices on others’ behalf, as in the Roman Mass. But Christ still gives elders to teach and shepherd (5:1–4): servants of the word among a priestly people, not priests between God and them.

Spiritual sacrifices. Our bodies (Romans 12:1), praise (Hebrews 13:15), doing good and sharing (Hebrews 13:16), and declaring his excellencies (v. 9). All acceptable only “through Jesus Christ”.

On a Tuesday. A mother cooking for a sick neighbour, a man thanking God on his commute, a teenager telling a friend about Jesus: each is offering a priestly sacrifice. There is no ordinary believer in God’s house.

verseByVerse.quote: For it stands in Scripture: "Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone, a cornerstone chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame." So the honor is for you who believe, but for those who do not believe, "The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone," and "A stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense." They stumble because they disobey the word, as they were destined to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scripture says God has laid a precious cornerstone in Zion, and whoever believes in him will never be put to shame. To believers he is precious, but to unbelievers he is the rejected stone that became the cornerstone, and a stone that makes them stumble. They stumble because they disobey the word, as they were destined to do.

Three stone texts. Isaiah 28:16: the cornerstone that sets the line of the whole building. Psalm 118:22: the rejected stone, quoted by Jesus (Matthew 21:42) and by Peter to the very council that rejected him (Acts 4:11). Isaiah 8:14: a stone of stumbling. The same stone is a foundation to some and an obstacle to others. The stone does not change; what differs is whether we build on it or trip over it.

“As they were destined to do”. Some read this as God appointing stumbling as the consequence of disobedience. Others, also in the Reformed tradition, read it more strongly: the disobedience itself falls within God’s purpose. Either way, Peter gives the reason first: “because they disobey the word”. Their refusal is truly theirs, and God’s purpose stands behind it. God is never the author of sin.

verseByVerse.quote: But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. Once you were not a people, but now you are God's people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s own possession, to declare the excellencies of the one who called you out of darkness into his wonderful light. Once you were not a people; now you are God’s people. Once you had not received mercy; now you have.

Israel’s titles. All four come from what God said to Israel (Exodus 19:5–6; Isaiah 43:20). Peter gives them, without qualification, to Gentiles with no race, priesthood, nation or possessions worth naming.

The purpose. To “proclaim the excellencies” of God: to publish them. The whole congregation is given the priestly task.

Has the church replaced Israel? Peter applies Israel’s calling to the church, Jew and Gentile together, because there is one people of God in Christ (Ephesians 2:11–22). That does not mean the Jewish people have no future in God’s purposes; Paul expects many to be grafted back in (Romans 11:23–26). Dispensational Christians keep Israel and the church more distinct; Reformed readers see one people, centred on Christ.

Hosea. Hosea named his children Not-My-People and No-Mercy, and God promised to reverse the names (Hosea 1:6–10; 2:23). Peter applies the reversal to Gentiles. Whatever they are called in their towns, God has renamed them.

On a Tuesday. A young believer from a broken home, with no sense of belonging anywhere, reads v. 10. Once not a people; now God’s people. Let her find her family in the church, and her voice in praising the God who called her.
verseByVerse.note: Titles once given to Israel at Sinai are now given to the church.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–25 — Submission, and the Steps of Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As foreigners and exiles, fight the desires that war against your soul, and live so well among unbelievers that their slander is silenced and they glorify God. Submit for the Lord’s sake to every human authority, even the emperor. Live as free people, as God’s servants. Slaves, submit even to unjust masters, because Christ suffered unjustly, leaving an example to trace. He did not retaliate, but entrusted himself to God. And he bore our sins in his body on the tree.
verseByVerse.theology:
Entrusting Rather Than Suppressing

Christ did not revile in return; he kept entrusting himself to the one who judges justly. Then he did what no follower can copy: he bore our sins in his body on the tree.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter spoke directly to slaves, and told believers to honour an emperor who would soon persecute them.

Now: Follow in his steps: do good, bear injustice without retaliation, and hand the case to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, I urge you as sojourners and exiles to abstain from the passions of the flesh, which wage war against your soul. Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As foreigners and exiles, keep away from the sinful desires that wage war against your soul. Live such good lives among unbelievers that, though they accuse you of wrongdoing, they will see your good deeds and glorify God on the day he visits.

An enemy within. A church under outside pressure tends to see all its danger outside. Peter names a nearer enemy: our own desires, campaigning against our soul.

Honourable. The word means beautiful, attractive: not merely correct, but winsome.

When, not if. The slander is expected. Christians were accused of atheism, cannibalism and disloyalty.

The day of visitation. Some read it as the day of judgment, when even unbelievers must acknowledge God. More likely, it means the day God visits them in mercy, when pagans who watched Christians’ lives come to faith and glorify him (Luke 19:44). It is Jesus’ own strategy: “let your light shine” (Matthew 5:16).

On a Tuesday. A colleague mocks your faith. You cannot win the argument today. But you can be the most honest, hardworking and kind person in the office. Peter expects slander to be answered by lives that make it obviously untrue.

verseByVerse.quote: Be subject for the Lord's sake to every human institution, whether it be to the emperor as supreme, or to governors as sent by him to punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good. For this is the will of God, that by doing good you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the Lord’s sake, submit to every human authority: the emperor, and the governors he sends to punish wrongdoers and praise those who do right. It is God’s will that by doing good you silence foolish people’s ignorant talk.

For the Lord’s sake. Not because the state deserves it, but because Christ requires it.

Which emperor. Very likely Nero, who within a few years would burn Christians, and under whom Peter would probably die. Peter is not describing an ideal government or making submission depend on good behaviour.

What it does not mean. Submission is not unconditional. Peter himself told the council, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). Where the state commands what God forbids, Christians must refuse, and accept the consequences.

Muzzle. “Put to silence” means to muzzle. The best answer to slander is a life that removes its material.
verseByVerse.note: The emperor at the time was probably Nero.

verseByVerse.quote: Live as people who are free, not using your freedom as a cover-up for evil, but living as servants of God. Honor everyone. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the emperor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Live as free people, but do not use your freedom as a cover for evil; live as God’s servants. Honour everyone, love the family of believers, fear God, honour the emperor.

Free and slaves. Peter says this to people he has just told to submit to Nero, and to slaves. His freedom is not political. Someone wholly owned by God is beyond anyone else’s ownership.

A cover-up. Christian freedom is never permission to sin.

Four commands. Honour everyone: radical in a society of rigid ranks. Love the brotherhood: warmer, for the family. Fear God: reserved for him alone. Honour the emperor: the same verb as for everyone. Caesar gets the honour due to every person, and not one degree of the fear due to God.

On a Tuesday. In an election season full of contempt, Peter’s four commands are a guide. Honour your opponents, love your fellow believers across party lines, fear God above all, and respect your leaders without worshipping them.

verseByVerse.quote: Servants, be subject to your masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust. For this is a gracious thing, when, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly. For what credit is it if, when you sin and are beaten for it, you endure? But if when you do good and suffer for it you endure, this is a gracious thing in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Slaves, submit to your masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle but also to the harsh. It is commendable before God when someone, aware of him, endures unjust suffering. There is no credit in enduring a beating you deserve, but if you suffer for doing good and endure it, God approves.

Real slaves. Household slaves, perhaps a third of the population. Peter speaks to them directly, as moral agents, which ancient moralists never did. That alone gives them dignity.

“Mindful of God”. What makes it grace is not the suffering, which alone is only misfortune, but that the sufferer keeps God in view through it.

Does the Bible approve of slavery? No. Peter addresses believers in the world as it was, without endorsing the system. Scripture sows the seeds of its overthrow: a slave is “a beloved brother” (Philemon 16), slaves should gain freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21), and “enslavers” are listed among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10).

What it does not mean today. An employee is not a slave. He can leave, seek legal protection and report wrongdoing. Nothing here requires anyone to stay in abuse or cover a crime. But the principle remains: work well, honour those over you even when unfair, and do not repay evil with evil.

On a Tuesday. Your manager takes credit for your work again. You may raise it calmly, or look for another job. But you do not need to sabotage, gossip or seethe. God sees, and endurance mindful of him is precious to him.

verseByVerse.quote: For to this you have been called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You were called to this, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example so that you would follow in his steps.

Called to it. The same word as being called out of darkness into light (2:9). One calling, two faces.

A copybook. “Example” (hypogrammos) is the line of letters a teacher wrote at the top of a page for a child to trace underneath. Discipleship is a child’s hand tracing the master’s letters, step by step.

Who writes this. Peter, who promised to follow Jesus to prison and death and did not, and who was told on the beach, “Follow me” (John 21:19). He knows how hard tracing those letters is.

verseByVerse.quote: He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. When insulted, he did not insult back; when he suffered, he made no threats, but kept entrusting himself to God, who judges justly.

Isaiah 53. Peter applies the suffering Servant, of all things, as instruction for slaves. The powerless are tempted to retaliation and to small deceits. Christ did neither.

An eyewitness. Peter was in the courtyard. The tenses suggest the insults kept coming and the silence kept holding.

No threats. A threat is the last weapon of someone with no other options. Christ had other options (Matthew 26:53).

Entrusting. The verb means to hand over, and it is continuous. He did not suppress the desire for justice; he transferred it to the Judge. That is what anyone without a court can do.

On a Tuesday. A friend spreads a lie about you. Everything in you wants to hit back. Instead, tell God the whole case, out loud if need be, and leave it with him. That is not weakness; it is trust in a just Judge.

verseByVerse.quote: He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ himself carried our sins in his body on the cross, so that we might die to sin and live for righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed.

Beyond example. Now Peter goes where no follower can follow. “Bore” is the word for carrying a sacrifice to the altar. “The tree” recalls Deuteronomy 21:23: cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. Christ went under the curse.

A moral aim. He bore our sins so that we would die to sin, not continue in it.

His wounds. The word means the welt left by a lash. Many of Peter’s readers had such marks. His stripes did what theirs never could.

What it does not mean. It is not a promise of physical healing in this life. In Isaiah and here, the healing is from sin, as the first half of the verse shows. Bodily healing will come fully at the resurrection.

For worship. Pause over the words “our sins… in his body”. He carried yours.

verseByVerse.quote: For you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You were like sheep going astray, but now you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.

Straying. Sheep do not run away on purpose. They drift, head down, one mouthful at a time, until the flock is gone (Isaiah 53:6).

Returned. The verb can be read as passive: you were turned back. Sheep do not find their own way home.

Shepherd and Overseer. Shepherd brings Psalm 23 and John 10. Overseer (episkopos) is the guardian who watches over. Peter gives the title first to Christ, and calls himself only a fellow elder (5:1).

Peter’s own story. He strayed in public and was brought back by a look in a courtyard and a breakfast on a beach.

On a Tuesday. If you have drifted from Christ, a little at a time, you do not need to find your own way back. Turn and call to the Shepherd. He is already looking for you.

3.title: Suffering for Righteousness: Wives, Husbands, and Christ's Victory
3.overview: Chapter 3 completes the household instructions for wives and husbands (vv. 1–7), calls the whole church to repay evil with blessing and to give a gentle reason for its hope (vv. 8–17), and grounds everything in Christ (vv. 18–22): his once-for-all death, his proclamation to the spirits in prison, his resurrection and his ascension to God’s right hand, with every power subject to him. The movement is from the household to the cosmos. Christ’s victory over every power is the ground for enduring any unjust suffering.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wives are to submit to their own husbands, so that unbelieving husbands may be won by their lives. Their beauty should be inward, a gentle and quiet spirit, precious to God, like the holy women of old who hoped in God and did not give way to fear. Husbands are to live with their wives with understanding, honouring them as fellow heirs of the grace of life, so that their prayers are not hindered.
verseByVerse.theology:
Reading This Passage Rightly

The Christ-pattern applies to wives and husbands alike. A believing wife may win an unbelieving husband by her conduct; a husband must honour his wife as a fellow heir of the grace of life.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A woman converted without her husband was in a precarious position.

Now: This is a text about witness in marriage, never about tolerating abuse.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, wives, be subject to your own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives, when they see your respectful and pure conduct.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same way, wives, submit to your own husbands, so that if any do not believe the word, they may be won over without words by the way their wives live, when they see your respectful and pure conduct.

“Likewise”. This follows the pattern of Christ (2:21–23), applied to slaves, wives and, in v. 7, husbands. No one in the household is exempt.

The situation. Wives married to unbelievers. A wife was expected to share her husband’s religion; a woman who became a Christian alone was in a precarious position.

Submit. The same word used of citizens (2:13) and of the whole church (5:5). It is not a claim about worth: v. 7 calls her a fellow heir. And it is to “your own” husband, not to men in general.

Without a word. She has probably already said it. What remains is a life he sees every day.

For all wives? Peter applies a pattern Paul also teaches (Ephesians 5:22–24; Colossians 3:18) to the hard case of an unbelieving husband. Egalitarian Christians read these texts as cultural accommodation for that time. The complementarian reading fits better, since Peter grounds it in “the holy women” of old (v. 5) and in Christ’s pattern, not in Roman custom.

What it does not mean. It never means obeying a command to sin (Acts 5:29). And it is not a text about enduring abuse. A wife in danger should seek safety and help from the church and the law. Anyone using this verse to keep a woman in danger is using it against its author.

On a Tuesday. A woman’s husband mocks her faith. She keeps going to church, prays for him, and serves him with kindness she does not feel. Years later he asks her, “What is it that keeps you going?” That question is what Peter hoped for.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not let your adorning be external—the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear— but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let your beauty be merely outward: elaborate hairstyles, gold jewellery or fine clothes. Let it be the hidden person of the heart, with the lasting beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is very precious to God.

What it does not mean. Peter is not forbidding clothes, braids or jewellery; otherwise the sentence would forbid clothing too. He is speaking about where a woman looks for her worth.

Imperishable. The same word as the inheritance (1:4) and the seed (1:23). Hair, gold and cloth all belong to what perishes.

Gentle and quiet. Gentle (praus) means strength under control, the word Jesus used of himself (Matthew 11:29). Quiet means settled, untroubled. Neither means timid, silent or without opinions.

Precious to God. In a home where she may not be valued, Peter tells her how she looks from the one point of view that lasts.

On a Tuesday. A teenage girl spends hours on her appearance and still feels ugly. This verse does not shame her; it frees her. Her real beauty is the kind God sees and treasures, and it will not fade.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is how the holy women who hoped in God used to adorn themselves, by submitting to their own husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. And you are her children, if you do good and do not fear anything that is frightening.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is how the holy women of the past who hoped in God made themselves beautiful, submitting to their husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham and called him lord. You are her daughters if you do what is right and do not give way to fear.

Hoped in God. Their composure came from where their hope was fixed.

Sarah. She called Abraham “my lord” (Genesis 18:12), an ordinary courtesy. She was not flawless: she laughed at God’s promise and treated Hagar harshly. Peter points to a woman whose hope in God held despite everything.

Her daughters. Gentile believers are given Israel’s ancestry again.

Without fear. The picture ends in courage. Her gentleness is not fragility. A woman who hopes in God can be calm in a hostile house because nothing in it finally frightens her.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same way, husbands, live with your wives with understanding, honouring them as the weaker partner and as heirs with you of the gracious gift of life, so that nothing will hinder your prayers.

Understanding. Literally “according to knowledge”: study your wife and know her. That rules out the husband who is present in the house and absent from the marriage.

Weaker vessel. Both are vessels; she is the weaker of two, most likely in physical strength. Peter makes that the reason for honour, not for control. Because she is more vulnerable to him, he owes her more care. That reverses the usual logic of power.

Fellow heirs. Equal standing, equal inheritance. Whatever “submit” means, it cannot mean she is worth less.

Hindered prayers. The word means blocked like a road. God takes the wife’s side against a husband who mistreats her.

On a Tuesday. A husband snaps at his wife over breakfast, then prays on the way to work and finds heaven silent. Peter would tell him to turn round, apologise, and honour her. God listens to men who treat their wives as his daughters.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All of you: be like-minded, sympathetic, loving, tender-hearted and humble. Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult, but with blessing, as Psalm 34 teaches: the Lord sees the righteous and hears their prayers. If you suffer for doing right, you are blessed. Do not fear your opponents, but honour Christ as Lord in your hearts, and be ready to give a reason for your hope, with gentleness and respect.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Forgotten Half of Verse 15

Repay evil with blessing. Be ready to give a reason for your hope — with gentleness and respect.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Slandered believers were told to fear the Lord, not their accusers.

Now: A life that raises questions, and answers them courteously, is the best reply to slander.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, all of you, have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, a tender heart, and a humble mind. Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary, bless, for to this you were called, that you may obtain a blessing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally, all of you, be united in mind, sympathetic, loving as family, tender-hearted and humble. Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult, but bless, because you were called to this, so that you may inherit a blessing.

Five qualities. All relational. Sympathy is literally “suffering with”. Humble mind was close to an insult in Greek; Christianity made it a virtue.

No returned insult. Not only violence is forbidden, but the retaliation the powerless actually use: the sharp word.

Bless. Not just restraint, but active good: speaking well of them and asking God to bless them (Luke 6:28).

Called to inherit blessing. Not a bargain, but a description: you have been given blessing, so blessing is what you hand on.

On a Tuesday. A neighbour writes a rude note about your bins. You draft a sharp reply. Peter says: bless instead. Bake something, knock on the door, and pray for him by name.

verseByVerse.quote: For "Whoever desires to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit; let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Psalm 34 says, whoever wants to love life and see good days must keep his tongue from evil and lies, turn from evil and do good, and pursue peace. The Lord watches the righteous and listens to their prayers, but sets his face against those who do evil.

The right psalm. David wrote it after escaping danger with no power of his own.

The tongue first. The first counsel to a man under attack is to control his speech.

Pursue peace. A hunting word: chase it. Peace is not passive.

Eyes and ears. God is watching and listening. That is why we can decline to hit back: the wrong has been noticed by someone who will deal with it (2:23).

verseByVerse.quote: Now who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good? But even if you should suffer for righteousness' sake, you will be blessed. Have no fear of them, nor be troubled,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who will harm you if you are eager to do good? But even if you suffer for doing right, you are blessed. Do not fear what they fear, and do not be troubled.

Hurt but not harmed. Usually a life of good disarms hostility (2:12). But Peter knows what happened to Jesus. They can hurt you; they cannot harm the part of you that matters.

Blessed. Jesus’ own beatitude (Matthew 5:10).

Isaiah 8. Judah feared an alliance against it; Isaiah told them to fear the LORD instead (Isaiah 8:12–13). Peter quotes it next.

What it does not mean. Not a demand to feel nothing. Isaiah did not say the danger was imaginary. It is a call not to let fear rule.

verseByVerse.quote: but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead, honour Christ as Lord and holy in your hearts. Always be ready to explain to anyone who asks the reason for your hope, but do it with gentleness and respect.

One fear displaces another. Isaiah said “the LORD of hosts”; Peter writes “Christ the Lord”. A clear statement that Jesus is the LORD of the Old Testament.

A defence. The word is apologia, a courtroom defence, sometimes literal for these readers.

Being asked. They are not going out to argue; someone has noticed their hope and asked. A life that raises no questions will not need this verse.

The hope in you. Personal testimony with reasons, thought through in advance.

The forgotten half. “With gentleness and respect.” An answer given harshly has not obeyed this verse, however correct it is.

On a Tuesday. A colleague asks why you seem calm despite your diagnosis. You have two minutes by the coffee machine. Tell her, simply and kindly, that Jesus rose from the dead and holds your future. Then listen.

verseByVerse.quote: having a good conscience, so that, when you are slandered, those who revile your good behavior in Christ may be put to shame. For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God's will, than for doing evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep a clear conscience, so that those who slander your good conduct in Christ will be ashamed. It is better, if God wills it, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil.

A life to stand on. A man with something to hide cannot give a straight answer about his hope.

Exposure. The slander is public, the life is public, and the gap between them shames the accuser.

In Christ. What is really attacked is Christ in them.

If God wills. Peter will not call unjust suffering an accident or the devil’s victory. It falls within God’s will, which is what makes it bearable.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — Christ's Suffering and Cosmic Victory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God. Put to death in the flesh, made alive in the Spirit, he proclaimed to the spirits in prison who disobeyed in Noah’s day, when eight were brought safely through water. Baptism corresponds to that, saving not by washing the body but as an appeal to God through Christ’s resurrection. Now he is at God’s right hand, with angels, authorities and powers subject to him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ’s Victory

Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God. Verses 19–20 are disputed, but no reading offers a second chance after death.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Noah's household of eight was a small minority brought safely through.

Now: Every power believers fear has already been made subject to the risen Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ suffered once for all for sins, the righteous one for the unrighteous, to bring you to God. He was put to death in the body but made alive in the Spirit.

Once. Hapax: once for all, never repeated (Hebrews 9:26). No sacrifice needs topping up.

The righteous for the unrighteous. Five words of substitution: one innocent in the place of many guilty.

To bring us to God. The verb is used of bringing someone into a king’s presence. The goal of the cross is not only safety or happiness, but God himself.

“Made alive in the spirit”. Some take it as Christ’s human spirit living on after death; others as the Holy Spirit who raised him (Romans 8:11). The more likely reading contrasts two spheres: put to death in the realm of the flesh, raised in the realm of the Spirit, into resurrection life.

For worship. Everything in salvation is arrangements for getting you to God. Let that move you to draw near today.

verseByVerse.quote: in which he went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison, because they formerly did not obey, when God's patience waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being prepared, in which a few, that is, eight persons, were brought safely through water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the Spirit, Christ went and made a proclamation to the spirits in prison, who disobeyed long ago while God waited patiently in Noah’s day as the ark was built, in which only eight people were saved through water.

A hard passage. Godly readers have differed for centuries. Three main views:

First, Christ, by his Spirit, preached through Noah to the people of his day, who are now dead and “in prison”. This fits the mention of Noah and avoids any second chance after death (Hebrews 9:27).

Second, the risen Christ announced his victory to fallen angels imprisoned for their sin in Noah’s time (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). In the New Testament, unqualified “spirits” almost always means spiritual beings; the verb is a herald’s word, not the word for preaching the gospel; and v. 22 ends with angels and powers subject to him.

Third, Christ descended to the dead between his death and resurrection. It has ancient support, but the text does not clearly say it.

Verdict. The second view has most in its favour. What no view allows is a second chance for the dead.

“He descended into hell”. The Apostles’ Creed is often linked with this verse. Calvin and the Heidelberg Catechism (Q. 44) understand the phrase of Christ’s hellish anguish on the cross; others, of his remaining under death until the third day. Peter’s words do not settle the creed’s meaning.

Eight. Noah was a tiny minority in a world against him, and God waited patiently while he built. The eight were not lost. Neither will a small, harassed church be.
verseByVerse.note: One of the hardest passages in the New Testament. Main views: Christ preached through Noah to the people of his day; or after his death he proclaimed victory to fallen angels imprisoned for the sins of Noah’s time.

verseByVerse.quote: Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you, not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This water symbolises baptism, which now saves you, not by removing dirt from the body, but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who has gone into heaven and is at God’s right hand, with angels, authorities and powers subject to him.

Corresponds. The word is antitype: what the earlier pattern pointed to. Judgment falls, water is the instrument, and a few are brought through into a new world.

Does baptism give new birth? Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some other Christians read “baptism… now saves you” that way. But Peter explains at once: “not as a removal of dirt from the body”. The water itself does nothing. What saves is what baptism expresses: “an appeal to God for a good conscience”, a heart turning to God, “through the resurrection of Jesus Christ”. Baptism saves as a wedding ring marries: it is the sign and pledge of a union whose power lies elsewhere. That is why, in the view of this app, baptism belongs to those who can make that appeal themselves.

Every power subject. Magistrate, mob, emperor, and whatever stands behind them: all named and placed beneath Christ, already.

On a Tuesday. A believer is anxious about a court case, a diagnosis, an unstable job. Read v. 22. Every authority over your life sits beneath the one who loved you and gave himself for you.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Likewise, wives, be subject to your own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives,<sup>2</sup>when they see your respectful and pure conduct.<sup>3</sup>Do not let your adorning be external—the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear—<sup>4</sup>but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious.<sup>5</sup>For this is how the holy women who hoped in God used to adorn themselves, by submitting to their own husbands,<sup>6</sup>as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. And you are her children, if you do good and do not fear anything that is frightening.<sup>7</sup>Likewise, husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.<sup>8</sup>Finally, all of you, have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, a tender heart, and a humble mind.<sup>9</sup>Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary, bless, for to this you were called, that you may obtain a blessing.<sup>10</sup>For "Whoever desires to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit;<sup>11</sup>let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it.<sup>12</sup>For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil."<sup>13</sup>Now who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good?<sup>14</sup>But even if you should suffer for righteousness' sake, you will be blessed. Have no fear of them, nor be troubled,<sup>15</sup>but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect,<sup>16</sup>having a good conscience, so that, when you are slandered, those who revile your good behavior in Christ may be put to shame.<sup>17</sup>For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God's will, than for doing evil.<sup>18</sup>For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit,<sup>19</sup>in which he went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison,<sup>20</sup>because they formerly did not obey, when God's patience waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being prepared, in which a few, that is, eight persons, were brought safely through water.<sup>21</sup>Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you, not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ,<sup>22</sup>who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him.

4.title: Stewards of Grace: The Meaning of Suffering
4.overview: Chapter 4 returns to suffering in the light of the end: “The end of all things is at hand” (v. 7). The first half (vv. 1–11) shows how suffering settles a believer’s break with the old life, and how a church facing the end should live: clear-headed for prayer, loving earnestly, hospitable, and using every gift for others. The second half (vv. 12–19) speaks directly to the fiery trial: do not be surprised; rejoice to share Christ’s sufferings; do not be ashamed to suffer as a Christian; and entrust your soul to a faithful Creator.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Stewards of God's Varied Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Since Christ suffered, arm yourselves with the same mind: suffering for him settles our break with sin. You have spent enough time living as pagans do; your old friends are puzzled and slander you, but they will answer to God. The end is near, so be clear-headed for prayer, love one another deeply, show hospitality without grumbling, and use each gift to serve others, so that God is glorified through Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
Stewards of God's Varied Grace

Suffering for Christ settles a believer's break with sin. Because the end is near, stay clear-headed for prayer, love earnestly, and use each gift to serve others.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Neighbours were baffled when converts no longer joined them, and spoke against them.

Now: Love covers a multitude of sins: it does not pass offences around.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin, so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since Christ suffered in his body, arm yourselves with the same attitude, because whoever has suffered in the body is done with sin, and lives the rest of his life for God’s will, not for human desires.

Armed with a thought. The weapon is a settled conviction: suffering is the road Christ took. Decide what suffering means before it comes, not during it.

“Ceased from sin”. Not that suffering makes us sinless; the commands that follow assume otherwise. Some refer it to Christ, who is done with sin after dealing with it once (3:18). More likely, it describes what suffering for Christ does to a believer: he has chosen under pressure, and the choice settles something. He has stopped negotiating with sin.

On a Tuesday. A young man loses a promotion because he refused to falsify figures. It hurt. But the pull of that kind of success has lost its grip on him. He has learnt what it was worth.

verseByVerse.quote: For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do, living in sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry. With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them in the same flood of debauchery, and they malign you;
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have spent enough time in the past doing what pagans do: sensuality, lust, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties and idolatry. They are surprised that you no longer join them in their reckless flood of excess, and they speak evil of you.

Enough. A dry understatement: you have given that more than enough of your life.

A social list. Every item was done in company, and much of it was part of temple worship. Leaving it cost friends.

Surprised. The neighbours are bewildered. When everyone is carried by a current, the one standing still feels like a criticism of all the others.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians must avoid unbelievers’ social occasions. Jesus ate with sinners (Luke 7:34), and we cannot leave the world (1 Corinthians 5:10). The issue is joining the excess. You may be at the party; you should not be part of what it becomes.

On a Tuesday. A new Christian stops going to Friday binges with his workmates. They tease him and stop inviting him. Peter would tell him to keep loving them, invite them to something else, and expect questions. Their surprise is an opening.

verseByVerse.quote: but they will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. For this is why the gospel was preached even to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they will give account to God, who is ready to judge the living and the dead. That is why the gospel was preached even to those now dead, so that though they were judged in the body as all people are, they might live in the spirit as God does.

Ready. The Judge is standing by. The delay is patience, not absence.

Preached to the dead? Some early writers read this as preaching to the dead in Hades, or link it with 3:19. The most likely reading is that the gospel was preached to believers while they were alive who have since died. Neighbours mocked: “Their faith did them no good; they died like everyone else.” Peter answers: they died, the judgment all flesh receives, but they live with God. Scripture gives no second chance after death (Hebrews 9:27).

For worship. At a Christian funeral, this verse speaks. Death passed its verdict on the body. It did not have the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: The end of all things is at hand; therefore be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The end of all things is near, so be clear-minded and self-controlled, so that you can pray.

The end. Telos: not merely the stopping but the goal. Things will not run out; they will arrive.

“At hand”. Two thousand years have passed. The New Testament never set a date; it called the church to live in readiness. Peter knew that with the Lord a day is as a thousand years (2 Peter 3:8).

A steady head. We might expect a call to dramatic action. Peter says: be sober and pray. A frightened, distracted or intoxicated mind cannot pray.

On a Tuesday. Most prayer fails not through unbelief but through clutter. Turn off the noise for ten minutes, clear your head, and pray. Peter treats that as preparation for the end.

verseByVerse.quote: Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins. Show hospitality to one another without grumbling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Above all, keep loving one another deeply, because love covers a multitude of sins. Show hospitality to one another without complaining.

Covers. From Proverbs 10:12. Not atonement (only Christ’s blood does that), and not concealment of crime. It means love does not spread offences, rehearse them or keep the account open. Small, persecuted churches meeting in homes produced constant friction; love decided whether they survived it.

What it does not mean. Love overlooks many small wrongs and forgives readily. But serious or unrepentant sin must be confronted (Matthew 18:15–17), and abuse and crime must be reported to the proper authorities (Romans 13:4). Covering sin in love never means hiding harm from those who need protecting.

Hospitality without grumbling. There were no church buildings; someone’s home took the wear, and travelling Christians needed beds. Peter knows the host household is most likely to resent it, and that resentment comes out as muttering.

On a Tuesday. Your small group meets at your house again, and the carpet is wearing. Peter says: open the door, and stop muttering about it. Your home is one of God’s tools.

verseByVerse.quote: As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace: whoever speaks, as one who speaks oracles of God; whoever serves, as one who serves by the strength that God supplies—in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each of you has received a gift; use it to serve others, as good stewards of God’s many-sided grace. Whoever speaks should speak as one speaking God’s words; whoever serves should do it with the strength God supplies, so that God is glorified in everything through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power for ever. Amen.

Each. Every believer has a gift. And it comes already assigned: for others.

Stewards. We manage what belongs to God and will give account. “Varied” means many-coloured, like embroidered cloth. A church of one colour has lost something God meant to be seen.

Speaking and serving. Word and deed. Those who speak in the church should handle it as God’s own words: carefully, not casually. Those who serve run on God’s supply, not their own reserves.

Prophecy today? Continuationists include prophecy and tongues among the speaking gifts here. Peter’s point is that whoever speaks in the church, teaching, preaching or exhorting, should speak “as one who speaks oracles of God” by faithfully passing on what God has said. The more likely reading is that this describes faithful handling of God’s revealed word, not new revelation.

For worship. Thinking rightly about gifts ends in doxology. The goal is not the gift, but God glorified.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not be surprised by the fiery trial, as though something strange were happening. Rejoice as you share Christ’s sufferings. If you are insulted for his name, the Spirit of glory rests on you. Do not suffer as a wrongdoer or a meddler; but if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed. Judgment begins with God’s household. So those who suffer by God’s will should entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and keep doing good.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgement Beginning at Home

Do not be surprised by the fiery trial. To suffer as a Christian is no shame; entrust your soul to a faithful Creator while doing good.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: “Christian” was probably an outsiders’ insult, and Peter told them to wear it.

Now: Make sure any suffering is for Christ’s name, not for wrongdoing or interfering.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dear friends, do not be surprised by the fiery trial that has come to test you, as if something strange were happening. Rejoice as you share in Christ’s sufferings, so that you will be overjoyed when his glory is revealed.

Do not be surprised. The same word as v. 4. Pagans are surprised at you; do not you be surprised at this.

The fiery trial. Literally “the burning”, the smelting word from 1:7. It has a purpose: to test.

The real danger. Not the suffering but how we read it: concluding that it is abnormal, that God has withdrawn, that others must be doing better. Peter says suffering is a normal part of the Christian life. Much of the pain of suffering is the suspicion that it should not be happening.

Insofar as. Joy is commanded for the share of suffering that is truly a share in Christ’s. And it is one joy in two instalments: begun under the fire, completed when his glory appears.

On a Tuesday. A believer loses friends over her faith and thinks something must be wrong with her. Peter would say: this is normal. Christ walked here first, and you are walking with him.

verseByVerse.quote: If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you are insulted because of Christ’s name, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory, God’s Spirit, rests on you.

For his name. Not for being tactless or difficult. Peter makes that distinction in the next verse.

Insult. Most Christians under pressure face not courts but contempt: a reputation quietly ruined.

The Spirit rests. The verb is from Isaiah 11:2, where the Spirit rests on the Messiah, and it recalls the glory-cloud that rested on the tabernacle. The presence that filled the tent rests on people being sworn at in the street.

A textual note. Some manuscripts add “and of power” after “glory”, and later ones add a sentence found in the KJV: “on their part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified.” Both are probably later additions. The meaning is unaffected.

verseByVerse.quote: But let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler. Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
None of you should suffer as a murderer, thief, criminal or meddler. But if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed; praise God that you bear that name.

Earned trouble. Peter will not let the blessing of v. 14 be claimed by a Christian who brought trouble on himself.

A meddler. The word may be Peter’s own coinage: someone who oversees other people’s business. Placed beside murder and theft, it is startling. A busybody in a suspected minority does real damage, then mistakes the hostility for persecution.

“Christian”. Used only three times in the New Testament, and probably an outsiders’ nickname first used at Antioch (Acts 11:26). Peter tells them to catch the insult and wear it.

On a Tuesday. Before calling your trouble persecution, ask honestly: is this for Christ, or for my sharp tongue, my laziness, or my interfering? If it is for Christ, do not be ashamed. If it is not, repent.
verseByVerse.note: “Christian” was first a nickname given by outsiders; it appears only three times in the New Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God? And "If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?" Therefore let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is time for judgment to begin with God’s household. If it starts with us, what will happen to those who do not obey the gospel? “If the righteous are saved with difficulty, what will become of the ungodly and sinners?” So those who suffer according to God’s will should entrust themselves to their faithful Creator and continue to do good.

Judgment begins at home. The idea comes from Ezekiel 9:6: “begin at my sanctuary”. Their suffering is not outside God’s plan; it is the first movement of his refining, and it starts with his people.

From lesser to greater. Peter leaves the question hanging. If God’s household goes through this, what of those who reject the gospel?

Scarcely saved. From Proverbs 11:31. Not saved by a narrow margin or with barely enough grace, but saved through difficulty. Salvation is certain; the road is hard.

Entrust. The deposit word, as Christ entrusted himself to the Judge (2:23). And God is called Creator, the only time in the New Testament. Hand your soul back to the one who made it. He is faithful; the deposit will be there. And do it “while doing good”: not instead of acting, but while acting.

On a Tuesday. A Christian facing a hostile tribunal at work prays before the meeting: “Faithful Creator, I give you my soul and my reputation.” Then she goes in and does her job well.
